The Lighthouse Log
For eleven years the keeper wrote one line in
the log at every change of watch, and most of
the lines say nothing more than the weather and
the state of the lamp. Read together, though,
they make a kind of diary, because a man who
writes the same sentence every four hours for
eleven years starts to notice what is differ-
ent about each one, and the differences are where
his life is written down.
In the first year the entries are short and
careful. The handwriting is the upright hand of
somebody who expects an inspector to read every
page, and the words are the words of the printed
instructions pasted inside the front cover.
By the third year the inspector has visited
twice and read nothing, and the entries have
begun to grow. The keeper notes the birds that
rest on the gallery rail, the ships he can name
from their lights alone, and once, in a whole
paragraph squeezed between two ruled lines, a
conversation with the boy who brought the
supplies from the harbour, who wanted to know
whether the light could be seen from the moon.
The keeper wrote that he had told the boy it
could not, and that he was no longer sure he
had told him the truth, since nobody had ever
gone to the moon to look.
The storms are recorded in a different way. In
a gale the entries become shorter again, and the
upright hand comes back, as if the keeper knew
that on those nights somebody might one day have
to read exactly what he had seen and done. Every
lamp trimmed, every hour the fog signal sounded,
every vessel seen in distress is there, with the
time to the minute and nothing else, and the next
morning the ordinary entries return as though the
night had been like any other.
The last entry is in another hand. It records
that the keeper was taken ill at the change of
the morning watch, that the lamp was extinguished
at sunrise as usual, and that the relief keeper
had arrived from the mainland by the afternoon

boat. The new keeper kept a log of his own, in a
new book, and the old one was sent to the board
in the city, where it sat in a cupboard for fifty
years before anybody thought to open it.
